title: Trust Recovery
concept: The Proof Protocol, for a real breach: the one who broke trust names it, you agree one change you’ll both be able to see, and you look at the record together at each check-in, feelings first.
whenToUse: After a betrayal, a lie or a string of broken agreements, or anything else that leaves a clear before and after in how safe things feel.
steps: Name what happened, clearly, without deflecting. The partner who broke trust names it and acknowledges the impact; the hurt partner is never asked to confess in return.
Decide on one specific change you can both see. Any transparency is offered voluntarily by the partner who broke trust, for a set time — it never becomes monitoring.
Set a real time window, and put the check-in dates in the calendar.
Keep a simple table — write down only the facts, and look at it together at the check-in.
Check in — the hurt partner’s feelings and questions come first; the record is an aid, never the judge. Then decide together whether to extend it, adjust it or close it out.
If it’s not safe, stop and get outside support.

phrases.text: What happened was ___. I’m not debating that.
My proof: ___. You’ll see it when ___.
Looking at the record: met / partial / missed.

working: B names what happened, the drinks with a colleague kept quiet, and makes no excuses. The proof: B mentions plans with that colleague before they happen. They check in weekly for four weeks, A’s feelings first. One week is only partly kept, and B owns it honestly. A says the check-ins are helping, so they agree to extend the window.
notWorking: Week two, B skips the heads-up and offers another long apology instead: “Can’t you just trust me again?” Or A pulls out the record mid-row to shame B. Demanding passwords, tracking location, or reading messages isn’t proof; it’s monitoring.
activity: Fill in one Proof row and the 4-week table together. Keep the Proof Protocol card beside you.
warn: If it’s not safe, stop and get outside support. Transparency is offered voluntarily by the partner who broke trust, is time-limited, and never becomes monitoring — no demanding passwords, location tracking, or reading messages. If refusing the “voluntary” transparency would feel unsafe, it isn’t voluntary: stop and use the Help Lines. If you can’t agree that a breach happened, this tool isn’t for it — get outside support.
note: Deciding not to rebuild, or to end the relationship, is a valid outcome of this protocol, not a failure of it.
